lessons.title: CSV import and declared column meaning
lessons.summary: If both declared column classes become numeric, how is ID 001 printed?
explanation: read.csv reads delimited text into a data frame. Here text supplies a tiny literal CSV rather than an external path. colClasses declares the ID as character and minutes as numeric, so leading zeros in an identifier are not mistaken for numeric magnitude.

An imported column still needs its meaning, missing-value policy and valid range checked. stringsAsFactors = FALSE makes the intended text treatment explicit. Never assume a plausible inferred type proves that units, IDs or measurements were interpreted correctly.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
data <- read.csv(text = "id,minutes\n001,15\n", colClasses = c("character", "numeric"),
                 stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
cat(data$id, "\n", sep = "")
cat(data$minutes, "\n", sep = "")

```

Expected output or behavior: 001
15. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: RDS serialization and trusted inputs
lessons.summary: If minutes changes to 20 before saving, what returns after reading?
explanation: saveRDS writes one R object, preserving R-specific structure such as classes and attributes; readRDS returns the object instead of choosing a variable name in the caller. Assign its result explicitly. This differs from a plain-text CSV interchange.

The fixture writes and reads its own local object. RDS is not a safe interchange boundary for arbitrary untrusted files and is not guaranteed portable forever across versions or systems. Validate the loaded shape and record provenance; do not execute unknown serialized content as a substitute for a documented data format.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
entry <- list(topic = "read", minutes = 15)
saveRDS(entry, "entry.rds")
restored <- readRDS("entry.rds")
cat(identical(entry, restored), "\n", sep = "")
cat(restored$minutes, "\n", sep = "")

```

Expected output or behavior: TRUE
15. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Paths connections and stream ownership
lessons.summary: If the text passed to write_note changes to rest, what is read after it returns?
explanation: A connection represents an input or output stream. file(path, open = "wt") opens a text-writing connection; close releases it. Inside a function, on.exit(close(con), add = TRUE) registers cleanup even if the body errors.

file.path joins path components using platform conventions, not an authorization policy. writeLines writes text lines to the connection; readLines reads them after the writer is closed. The example owns a disposable relative path and never accepts a user-supplied traversal path.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
write_note <- function(path, text) {
  con <- file(path, open = "wt")
  on.exit(close(con), add = TRUE)
  writeLines(text, con)
}
path <- file.path(".", "note.txt")
write_note(path, "read")
cat(readLines(path), "\n", sep = "")

```
Expected output or behavior: read. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Explain why file.path alone cannot authorize a requested filesystem destination. You may trace it without a R interpreter; reading completion is not proof of a local run.

lessons.title: Assertions and approximate equality
lessons.summary: If the expected value becomes 0.4 with the same tiny tolerance, what happens?
explanation: Floating-point arithmetic can differ from ideal decimal arithmetic. all.equal compares approximately but returns either TRUE or a descriptive character result, not simply FALSE on mismatch. Wrap it in isTRUE for a single logical condition.

stopifnot stops when a supplied condition is not TRUE. Use tolerance appropriate to the quantity and its scale, not a tolerance so large that a wrong result passes. This arithmetic check is not a statistical uncertainty interval.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
actual <- 0.1 + 0.2
ok <- isTRUE(all.equal(actual, 0.3, tolerance = 1e-12))
stopifnot(ok)
cat(ok, "\n", sep = "")

```
Expected output or behavior: TRUE. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Random seeds and sampling
lessons.summary: If both sample sizes change to 2, which properties hold?
explanation: set.seed initializes the random-number generator state. sample selects values, with replace = FALSE giving sampling without replacement. unique removes duplicate values, so length(unique(first)) counts distinct sampled values. Resetting the same seed before the same operation reproduces its sequence in the same relevant runtime/RNG configuration.

A fixed seed does not make a convenience sample unbiased or make simulated data real evidence. Record R and RNG versions for reproducibility, and do not compare only one random outcome to justify a method. Here equality is checked rather than relying on an unexplained fixed random vector.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
set.seed(42)
first <- sample(1:10, size = 4, replace = FALSE)
set.seed(42)
second <- sample(1:10, size = 4, replace = FALSE)
cat(identical(first, second), "\n", sep = "")
cat(length(unique(first)), "\n", sep = "")

```

Expected output or behavior: TRUE
4. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Location summaries and outliers
lessons.summary: If the last value becomes 90, what changes?
explanation: mean adds values and divides by count; median is the middle ordered value, averaging the two central values for even length. Extreme values can move the mean substantially while leaving the median relatively stable.

An outlier is not automatically an error to delete. Check units, collection process and the intended population before choosing exclusions. These values are synthetic minutes and only illustrate arithmetic; neither summary alone describes the whole distribution.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
minutes <- c(10, 10, 10, 50)
cat(mean(minutes), "\n", sep = "")
cat(median(minutes), "\n", sep = "")
```

lessons.title: Spread quantiles and units
lessons.summary: If every value is multiplied by 2, what happens to sd and IQR?
explanation: sprintf("%.1f", x) formats a number as text with one decimal place; it changes display, not the stored number. sd estimates sample standard deviation using denominator n - 1; its unit matches the observations. var is its square and has squared units. quantile estimates cut points; R supports several definitions, so type = 7 is explicit here.

IQR is the difference between upper and lower quartiles. Multiplying all observations by a constant scales sd and IQR by its absolute value and variance by its square. For very small samples, spread estimates are unstable and conventions matter. Removing missing values changes the observations summarized and must follow a stated policy, not merely silence NA output.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
x <- c(1, 2, 3)
cat(sprintf("%.1f", sd(x)), "\n", sep = "")
cat(sprintf("%.1f", IQR(x, type = 7)), "\n", sep = "")

```

Expected output or behavior: 1.0
1.0. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Probability distributions and parameters
lessons.summary: If both threshold and mean change to 20, with sd still 2, what is the cumulative probability?
explanation: R commonly uses d for density or mass, p for cumulative probability, q for quantiles and r for random generation. pnorm(q, mean, sd) gives the probability at or below q under a specified normal model; a continuous density value is not the probability of one exact point.

A nondegenerate normal model is symmetric around its mean and has positive standard deviation; R also supports the special sd = 0 point-mass boundary, which is not used here. A calculation under that model does not establish that a real dataset is normal. Here the threshold equals the model mean, so half the probability lies below it.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
probability <- pnorm(10, mean = 10, sd = 2)
cat(sprintf("%.3f", probability), "\n", sep = "")

```
Expected output or behavior: 0.500. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Confidence intervals and repeated sampling
lessons.summary: If the other confidence level becomes 0.90 instead of 0.99, is it wider than the 0.95 interval?
explanation: t.test(x)$conf.int gives a t-based interval for a population mean. Under its sampling/model assumptions, a 95% confidence procedure covers the fixed true mean in 95% of repeated samples; it is not a statement that 95% of individual future values lie in this realized interval.

For the same data and method, a higher confidence level produces a wider interval. The method depends on independent observations and a suitable mean-sampling model, especially with tiny samples. Synthetic numbers here demonstrate the computation, not scientific adequacy.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
x <- c(8, 9, 10, 11, 12)
base <- t.test(x, conf.level = 0.95)$conf.int
other <- t.test(x, conf.level = 0.99)$conf.int
width <- function(interval) interval[2] - interval[1]
cat(width(other) > width(base), "\n", sep = "")

```
Expected output or behavior: TRUE. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Hypothesis tests and assumptions
lessons.summary: If mu becomes 0 for this same sample, which claim follows from a TRUE threshold check?
explanation: A one-sample t.test compares a mean with mu under its model assumptions. The p-value is the probability, under the null model, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed; it is not the probability that the null is true or that a result happened by chance.

Here the sample mean equals the tested null mean, producing p = 1. A threshold comparison alone is not practical importance, a causal conclusion or proof of no effect. Consider design, independence, distributional assumptions, multiple testing and effect size; five synthetic values do not validate a real study.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
x <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
result <- t.test(x, mu = 3)
cat(result$p.value < 0.05, "\n", sep = "")

```
Expected output or behavior: FALSE. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Correlation and causal limits
lessons.summary: If y is negated, what correlation and causal conclusion follow?
explanation: cor(x, y) defaults to Pearson correlation, a unitless measure of linear association between paired observations. It ranges from -1 to 1 when defined; zero variance or unsuitable missingness handling can make a calculation undefined or misleading.

A strong correlation can arise from confounding, reverse direction or design artifacts. Do not infer that changing x causes y to change. The constructed straight-line data isolate sign, not real-world validity; inspect shape and sampling context in actual analysis.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
x <- 1:4
y <- c(2, 4, 6, 8)
cat(sprintf("%.1f", cor(x, y)), "\n", sep = "")

```

lessons.title: Linear models and formula terms
lessons.summary: If every y value is doubled, how do the intercept and slope change?
explanation: lm(y ~ x, data = data) fits a linear response model with an intercept and x term by least squares. The tilde separates response from predictors; + adds terms in a formula, and y ~ 1 is an intercept-only model rather than the arithmetic assignment y = 1.

coef extracts fitted coefficients: intercept first and x slope next here. The slope describes a fitted change in mean y per unit x under the model, not automatically a causal effect. With the predictor design fixed, multiplying every response by a constant multiplies all least-squares coefficients by that constant. Tiny synthetic data can demonstrate fitting without validating the linear-model assumptions.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
data <- data.frame(x = 1:5, y = c(2, 4, 5, 4, 5))
fit <- lm(y ~ x, data = data)
cat(sprintf("%.1f", coef(fit)), sep = "\n")
cat("\n")

```

Expected output or behavior: 2.2
0.6. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Prediction uncertainty and extrapolation
lessons.summary: If chosen uses interval = "prediction", what does the width comparison show?
explanation: predict.lm with interval = "confidence" estimates uncertainty about the conditional mean response. interval = "prediction" additionally accounts for variation in one future observation under the fitted model, so it is wider here. Both depend on assumptions, not just successful software execution.

newdata supplies predictor values in a data frame. Its x = 3 is inside the observed range 1..5. Predictions far outside that range can be scientifically unreliable even if R returns a number. The returned matrix has fit, lwr and upr columns.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
data <- data.frame(x = 1:5, y = c(2, 4, 5, 4, 5))
fit <- lm(y ~ x, data = data)
point <- data.frame(x = 3)
mean_interval <- predict(fit, point, interval = "confidence")
chosen <- predict(fit, point, interval = "confidence")
width <- function(x) x[1, "upr"] - x[1, "lwr"]
cat(width(chosen) > width(mean_interval), "\n", sep = "")

```
Expected output or behavior: FALSE. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Residual diagnostics and model limitations
lessons.summary: If the formula becomes y ~ x - 1, must residuals still sum to zero?
explanation: residuals(fit) extracts discrepancies between responses and fitted means. In ordinary least squares with an intercept, their sum is approximately zero by the fitting equations; that arithmetic property is not evidence that every modeling assumption holds.

Residual-versus-fitted patterns may suggest nonlinearity or unequal variance; a Q-Q plot can reveal departures from a normal-error model. Checks cannot prove independence, exclude confounding or certify a small sample. In an R model formula, - 1 removes the intercept. Removing the intercept changes the zero-sum property, not just a display label.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
data <- data.frame(x = 1:5, y = c(2, 4, 5, 4, 5))
fit <- lm(y ~ x, data = data)
cat(abs(sum(residuals(fit))) < 1e-10, "\n", sep = "")

```
Expected output or behavior: TRUE. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Factor contrasts in a model
lessons.summary: If the reference becomes B, what are the intercept and A-versus-B coefficient?
explanation: A factor represents categories, not the numeric magnitudes of its internal codes. Under treatment contrasts, the first level is the reference: the intercept is its fitted group mean and the other coefficient is a difference from that mean.

factor(levels = c("A", "B")) and an explicit contr.treatment setting make coding visible. relevel changes the reference category, changing coefficient interpretation without changing the fitted group means. These group differences are descriptive, not automatically effects of an intervention.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
data <- data.frame(group = factor(c("A", "A", "B", "B"), levels = c("A", "B")),
                   y = c(2, 4, 6, 8))
data$group <- relevel(data$group, ref = "A")
fit <- lm(y ~ group, data = data, contrasts = list(group = "contr.treatment"))
cat(sprintf("%.1f", coef(fit)), sep = "\n")
cat("\n")

```

Expected output or behavior: 3.0
4.0. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Logistic models and link scales
lessons.summary: If type becomes link, is the printed -1.099 a negative probability?
explanation: glm with family = binomial() uses the logit link by default for a binary response. A 0/1 vector records failures/successes. The linear predictor is log-odds, log(p / (1 - p)); it is not itself a probability.

predict(type = "response") converts the linear predictor to probabilities, while type = "link" returns log-odds here. This intercept-only example estimates one shared probability. Separation, convergence, sample size and calibration matter in real models; four synthetic outcomes cannot validate risk predictions.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
data <- data.frame(success = c(0, 0, 0, 1))
fit <- glm(success ~ 1, data = data, family = binomial())
value <- predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(row = 1), type = "response")
cat(sprintf("%.3f", value), "\n", sep = "")

```
Expected output or behavior: 0.250. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Graphics devices and file output
lessons.summary: If the y-axis label changes to Seconds without converting the values, what changes?
explanation: pdf opens a headless file graphics device; plot sends drawing commands to the active device. dev.off closes it and finalizes the PDF. A function with on.exit(dev.off(), add = TRUE) makes cleanup occur even if plotting fails.

The fixture creates one synthetic scatterplot in plot.pdf. main is its title; xlab and ylab are axis labels; pch chooses a point symbol. No GUI display, browser execution or publication is implied. Check the generated artifact rather than treating printed success as visual verification.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
draw <- function() {
  pdf("plot.pdf", width = 5, height = 4)
  on.exit(dev.off(), add = TRUE)
  plot(1:3, c(2, 4, 3), main = "Synthetic study points",
       xlab = "Session index", ylab = "Minutes", pch = 19)
}
draw()
cat(file.exists("plot.pdf"), "\n", sep = "")

```

lessons.title: Histograms boxplots and scatterplots
lessons.summary: If breaks become c(0, 1, 4), what bin counts result?
explanation: hist bins a numeric distribution, boxplot summarizes center/spread and flagged extremes, and plot(x, y) shows paired values. par(mfrow = c(1, 3)) arranges three panels; it changes layout rather than the data.

With explicit equal-width breaks and right = TRUE, bins are right-closed; include.lowest includes the lowest endpoint. For unequal-width breaks, hist defaults to density so bar areas, not raw heights, represent proportions. The example compares bin counts, not just a decorative image. Boxplot flagged points are not automatically bad data, and scatterplot association is not causation.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
draw <- function() {
  pdf("plot.pdf", width = 10, height = 4)
  on.exit(dev.off(), add = TRUE)
  par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
  x <- c(1, 2, 3, 4)
  h <- hist(x, breaks = c(0, 2, 4), right = TRUE, include.lowest = TRUE,
            main = "Minutes distribution", xlab = "Minutes")
  boxplot(x, main = "Minutes spread", ylab = "Minutes")
  plot(seq_along(x), x, main = "Paired observations",
       xlab = "Session index", ylab = "Minutes", pch = 19)
  h$counts
}
counts <- draw()
cat(counts, sep = ",")
cat("\n")

```
Expected output or behavior: 2,2. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Profiling and measured optimization
lessons.summary: If n changes to 100, which claim is supported?
explanation: system.time evaluates an expression and reports measured CPU and elapsed time. Rprof samples execution for profiling, and Rprof(NULL) stops profiling. Short work may produce no useful samples; timings vary by runtime, load and hardware, so this example never asserts a specific duration or speedup.

Profiling identifies where time is spent, not which result is correct. Compare outputs and representative workloads before changing algorithms; warm-up and repeated measurements may matter. This bounded example writes a local profile file and verifies only the computed result plus a nonnegative elapsed measurement.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
measure <- function(n) {
  Rprof("profile.out")
  on.exit(Rprof(NULL), add = TRUE)
  timing <- system.time(total <- sum(seq_len(n)))
  cat(total, "\n", sep = "")
  cat(timing[["elapsed"]] >= 0, "\n", sep = "")
}
measure(1000)

```

TRUE. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Language objects and trusted evaluation
lessons.summary: If context$x becomes 9 before eval, what value results?
explanation: quote captures an R expression without evaluating it. eval evaluates that expression in a supplied environment; new.env(parent = baseenv()) gives this example a controlled lookup context for a known expression, not a security sandbox.

The expression here is authored directly as x + 1 and x is explicitly bound. Parsing arbitrary text and evaluating it can run arbitrary R operations; an environment or an allowlist of variable names alone does not make unknown code safe. Prefer a data format and explicit operations for external input.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
expression <- quote(x + 1)
context <- new.env(parent = baseenv())
context$x <- 4
cat(eval(expression, envir = context), "\n", sep = "")

```

lessons.title: Reproducible sessions and configuration
lessons.summary: If temporary digits becomes 5, does it leak after the function returns?
explanation: sessionInfo records the R version, platform and loaded package information. RNGkind describes random-generator configuration; options can also affect behavior and formatting. Saving metadata helps explain a run but does not by itself recreate dependencies, input data or operating-system behavior.

options returns prior values for changed settings, so a function can register on.exit(options(old), add = TRUE). This keeps local formatting from leaking into later analysis. Rscript --vanilla avoids startup files and workspace restoration, but still needs explicit data, package versions and seed policy.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
show_value <- function() {
  old <- options(digits = 3)
  on.exit(options(old), add = TRUE)
  cat(getOption("digits"), "\n", sep = "")
}
before <- getOption("digits")
show_value()
cat(identical(before, getOption("digits")), "\n", sep = "")
info <- sessionInfo()
cat(is.list(info), "\n", sep = "")

```

TRUE
TRUE. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: A bounded data-analysis pipeline
lessons.summary: If the first value becomes 65, what is retained and summarized?
explanation: A bounded pipeline checks type, missingness and domain before summarizing. Here input is a finite numeric vector; is.finite excludes NA, NaN and infinities, and the accepted range is 1..60 minutes. head(valid, 3) caps the number of retained valid observations.

The retained count and arithmetic mean describe only accepted observations in this synthetic input. They do not establish a population mean, causality or real-world validity. Real analysis also needs units, provenance, input-size limits and an explicit exclusion policy; silently dropping data can bias conclusions.
